nameStory: The Common Five-lined Skink gets its name from the five bright stripes that run down its back and sides, especially visible in young skinks. These lines are like nature's racing stripes, making this little lizard one of the most distinctively patterned reptiles in New England. The word 'skink' comes from the Greek word 'skinkos,' which ancient peoples used to describe these smooth, shiny lizards.
description: The Common Five-lined Skink is a sleek, smooth-scaled lizard that's about the size of your hand when fully grown, typically 5-8 inches long including its tail. Young skinks are jet black with five brilliant yellow or white stripes running from head to tail, plus a bright blue tail that looks almost electric. As they age, the stripes fade and adults become more brownish or grayish, with males developing orange-red coloring on their heads during breeding season. These are active, quick-moving lizards that you're more likely to see darting under logs than basking in the open.

idTips.label: Pattern
idTips.description: Young skinks display five distinct light-colored stripes running lengthwise down a dark body, feeling smooth and almost slippery to the touch if you manage to catch one

idTips.label: Scales
idTips.description: Scales are small, overlapping, and incredibly smooth - like touching polished metal or glass rather than the rougher texture of other lizards

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Adults reach 5-8 inches total length, with the tail making up about half that length - roughly the size of a large adult's palm

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Lightning-fast movements with quick stops and starts, often rustling through dry leaves with a distinctive scratchy sound before disappearing under cover

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found under logs, rocks, or leaf litter in wooded areas, often leaving a faint musky scent where they've been hiding

habitat: Common Five-lined Skinks prefer deciduous and mixed forests with plenty of fallen logs, rock piles, and leaf litter to hide under. They're particularly fond of areas with rotting stumps and woodpiles where they can hunt for insects and find shelter. In New England, look for them in oak-hickory forests and woodland edges, especially on south-facing slopes that get good sun exposure.

seasonality.spring: Active skinks emerge from winter hiding spots under logs and rocks, often basking in sunny patches. This is when you're most likely to spot them as they're less wary after winter dormancy.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity time with adults breeding and young skinks showing their brightest blue tails and yellow stripes. They're most active in morning and late afternoon, hiding during the hottest part of the day.
seasonality.fall: Skinks are busy feeding heavily before winter, making them slightly more visible as they forage. Young-of-the-year skinks are reaching adult size but still show some striping.
seasonality.winter: Hidden deep under logs, rocks, or in underground burrows in a state called brumation - essentially reptile hibernation. You won't see them active during cold months.

funFact: When grabbed by a predator, a Five-lined Skink can detach its bright blue tail, which continues to wiggle violently for several minutes while the skink escapes - and the tail will actually grow back over time, though never quite as colorful as the original!
confusionNotes: Young Five-lined Skinks are sometimes mistaken for salamanders due to their dark, moist-looking appearance, but skinks have dry, scaly skin while salamanders feel wet and smooth. Remember: if it's slippery but scaly with distinct stripes, it's a skink - if it's truly slimy and smooth, it's a salamander.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Common' Five-lined Skinks, they're actually quite uncommon in New England, representing the northern edge of their range. Many New Englanders have never seen one, making any sighting quite special and worth reporting to local nature organizations.
compareHints: The Common Five-lined Skink is the only native skink species in New England, making identification easier once you know what a skink looks like. Unlike other small lizards you might find (which would likely be escaped pets), native skinks have that distinctive smooth, overlapping scale pattern and the classic five-stripe design in juveniles. Other small reptiles in the region are either salamanders (which feel slimy) or snakes (which have no legs).
